blocks.text: The hidden cost of multitasking in IT support

When you are managing distractions during remote support calls, you are often paying a cognitive tax. Every time you switch from a terminal window to a Slack message, your brain has to perform a goal shift. This process is not instant. It requires deactivating the rules of your previous task and loading the rules for the new one. For a technician, this means you might be jumping between TeamViewer, a ticketing system, and documentation. If you do this hundreds of times a day, your brain never fully settles into a deep work state. This leads to the attention residue effect, where part of your focus remains stuck on the last ticket while you try to solve a new one.
Why IT technicians struggle with focus

The nature of the job is reactive. You are expected to be available for walk-ups, urgent phone calls, and high-priority tickets. This creates a fragmented environment. You rarely get an hour of uninterrupted time to focus on complex troubleshooting. When you are on a remote support call, your screen is often cluttered with diagnostic tools. If a notification pops up, it breaks your flow instantly. You lose the mental thread of the troubleshooting steps you just performed. This increases the chance of errors, such as misconfiguring a system or missing a detail in a ticket log.

items: Goal shifting requires significant mental energy.
Rule activation for different apps slows down your response time.

Fragmented tool landscapes lead to hundreds of switches daily.

blocks.text: You do not need expensive software to improve your focus. Start by using the built-in features on your Mac. Go to System Settings > Focus and create a custom mode for Support Calls. Set this to silence all notifications except from your team leads or critical monitoring tools. This prevents the ping of a new ticket from pulling your attention away during a screen-sharing session.

When you are on a call, use the ⌘ ⌥ ⌃ ⇧ shortcut to quickly toggle your Focus mode if you need to check an urgent alert. You can also set your status in Slack to 'On a call' to manage expectations with your team.
blocks.title: Use system-level focus

blocks.text: Another effective strategy is task batching. Instead of checking your ticketing queue every five minutes, set a timer for 45 minutes of deep troubleshooting. Use the remaining 15 minutes to clear your queue, update logs, and respond to messages. This reduces the frequency of your context switches and allows you to finish one task before starting the next. If you are worried about missing an emergency, set a specific sound for urgent tickets in your ticketing app and keep all other notifications off during your focus blocks.
How to handle the cognitive load

Managing distractions during remote support calls is also about how you handle information. Do not try to keep everything in your head. Use a simple text file or a scratchpad app to keep notes on the current call. When you feel the urge to switch apps, write down the next step in your scratchpad. This acts as an external memory, so you do not have to keep the entire troubleshooting plan in your working memory. If you need to search for a solution, use a tool that allows you to find information without opening a new browser tab or context switching away from your remote access app.

faq.question: Does macOS Focus mode really help?
faq.answer: Yes. It stops notifications from appearing on your screen, which prevents the visual trigger that leads to impulsive context switching.

faq.question: How do I stop checking Slack during a call?
faq.answer: Set your status to 'On a call' and turn off Slack notifications for the duration of your shift. Only allow notifications from specific, urgent channels.

faq.question: Is it better to multitask or single-task?
faq.answer: Single-tasking is significantly better. Research shows that multitasking reduces your effective IQ and increases the time needed to complete tasks.

costs.title: Productivity loss
costs.text: Chronic multitasking can reduce your actual productive time by up to 40 percent.

costs.title: Cognitive fatigue
costs.text: Constant context switching leads to mental exhaustion, making it harder to solve complex problems by the end of the day.

costs.title: Higher error rates
costs.text: Fragmented attention increases the likelihood of missing critical details in tickets or misconfiguring systems.

causes.title: Goal shifting
causes.text: Your brain spends energy deactivating one task and loading the rules for another every time you switch apps.

causes.title: Fragmented tool landscape
causes.text: Using 4 to 6 different apps per ticket creates a high volume of context switches that are difficult to avoid.

causes.title: Constant notifications
causes.text: Unfiltered alerts from Slack, email, and ticketing systems pull your attention away from the primary task.

fixes.title: Use macOS Focus modes
fixes.text: Configure a custom Focus mode that silences all non-essential notifications while you are on a remote support call.

fixes.title: Practice task batching
fixes.text: Group similar tasks, like password resets or log updates, into specific time blocks to reduce the number of goal shifts.

fixes.title: Use external scratchpads
fixes.text: Keep a simple text file open to note the next step in your troubleshooting process so you do not have to remember it while switching windows.
